SPLIT FINDING — shore side is a documented direction-test NO, but the vessel side is undocumented, and per the fuel gate (unstated fuel = INSUFFICIENT, never NO) the terminal verdict is INSUFFICIENT. Shore side (green): the Hadera FSRU (Excelsior, 2013-2022; a submerged-buoy deepwater mooring, Israel's first LNG import point) fed regasified gas into Israel Natural Gas Lines' (INGL) national transmission grid, which in turn supplies gas to essentially all of Israel's major power stations (~70% of national generation), not a single dedicated on-site plant. Regasification heat itself is met by boiler steam (closed loop) or seawater (open loop) — thermal, not electric, per the heat-is-not-power rule, so it would not count as captive power even setting the direction test aside. EVIDENCE: Georgetown Journal of International Affairs (2020): INGL's ~700 km transmission system 'supply[ies] high-pressure natural gas to major consumers such as electric power generators,' with gas from Hadera entering this shared grid in 2013; Global Energy Observatory's Hadera Deepwater LNG Terminal entry corroborates the buoy/grid-injection design; GE Vernova's Israel Electric Orot Rabin case study confirms IEC's Hadera-area Orot Rabin plant runs on this national gas supply via its own GE 9HA conversion, i.e. Orot Rabin is a grid offtaker of common-carrier gas, not a captive plant built to serve the terminal. VESSEL SIDE (the open half): Riviera documents the Energy Bridge class design as carrying 'an oversize boiler to provide the steam and power necessary to sustain vessel operations and the shipboard regasification process' — the Excelsior self-powers via its steam plant — but no source found states what fuel that plant burns (BOG/dual-fuel vs. fuel oil), so the fuel gate blocks both YES and NO on the vessel half.
